events.title: Free Panel: Bay Area Protest Photojournalists + Pop-Up Exhibit (SF Main Library)
events.description:
Steve DisenhofPhotojournalists on the Front Lines of Protest: A panel discussion hosted by Indivisible San Francisco and Pro Bono Photo.
Indivisible SF presents a panel of local photojournalists from Pro Bono Photo and other news organizations who will share selections from their portfolios and discuss the role photojournalism plays in documenting protest, civic action and pro-democracy movements.
From the civil rights and voting rights movements of the 1960s to today’s social justice actions, the San Francisco Bay Area has long been a significant site of protest and civil disobedience. Who documents these fleeting moments of protest and civic action? Local photojournalists share their experiences covering pro-democracy movements and street demonstrations throughout the Bay Area.

Hear firsthand accounts from photographers documenting recent protests and demonstrations, view a curated projection of their work and engage directly with the panelists during an audience Q&A.
Pop-Up Gallery: A selection of photographs by participating photojournalists will be displayed alongside historical protest photography from SFPL collections, connecting contemporary documentation of Bay Area demonstrations with the Library’s photographic record of protest and civic action. The display will be on view on the 4th Floor of the Main Library from Sept. 17–Dec. 31.
Moderator

ABOUT STREET SMART: LESSONS FROM A TV ICON
Directed by Ernie Bustamante | USA
This feature documentary tells the story of Sonia Manzano, beloved by millions as “Maria” from SESAME STREET. The film traces Sonia’s remarkable journey, from a young girl in the South Bronx who found refuge in television to becoming the first Latina to portray a regular character on American television. It celebrates her 44 years on SESAME STREET and her evolution into the creator of ALMA’S WAY. Featuring interviews with luminaries, original animation, and scripted scenes infused with humor and heart, this inspirational documentary invites audiences to rediscover the wisdom and enduring impact of a beloved television icon.

events.title: B-Movie: Lust & Sound in West-Berlin
events.description:
© DEF Media GmbHJoin us for a filmscreening of B-Movie: Lust & Sound in West-Berlin:
Hoping to follow in the footsteps of legends like David Bowie and CAN, Manchester punk rocker and early electronic music acolyte Mark Reeder arrives in a divided Berlin in 1979. Luckily, he films everything he sees: black leather-clad teenagers, giant pink and red hairdos, gritty basement gigs, and a parade of the scene’s most illustrious figures, including Nick Cave, Mania D’s Gudrun Gut, and Einstürzende Neubauten’s Blixa Bargeld. From the movement’s system-smashing highs to its waning years in the age of reunification, Reeder is the outsider with an insider’s view of the beating heart of Germany’s underground cultural life.
Lovingly assembled from a decade of fascinating film and audio material, B-Movie: Lust & Sound in West-Berlin provides a fast-paced but no less intimate look at Berlin’s punk and electronic subculture through the eyes of one of its greatest devotees. Winner of the Heiner Carow Prize at the 2015 Berlin International Film Festival.

With Mark Reeder, Marius Weber, Gudrun Gut, Annette Humpe, Blixa Bargeld, Nick Cave, Nena, and Christiane F.

The end is the beginning. Moving backwards and forwards, Betrayal illuminates a seven-year affair between Emma and Jerry, her husband Robert’s closest friend. As the story unravels, the tension between memory and reality is sharpened, revealing shifting perspectives, hidden motives, unspoken power dynamics, and titillating pleasure behind the deception. Laced with Pinter’s signature wit, this piercing drama is a masterclass in what is said — and unsaid — between lovers and friends. Words and silences punctuate the irreversible consequences of long-concealed truths and betrayals which reverberate far beyond a single act. After helming hit Marin Theatre productions of The Cherry Orchard and Waste, A.C.T. Artistic Director Emerita Carey Perloff returns to Marin Theatre to direct.

Japanese Tea Garden’s Free Admission Hour (Golden Gate Park)
Japanese Tea Garden
The Japanese Tea Garden provides visitors from around the world with an opportunity to experience the natural beauty, tranquility, and harmony of a Japanese-style garden in the heart of San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park.
Originally created as a “Japanese Village” exhibit for the 1894 California Midwinter International Exposition, the Japanese Tea Garden endures as one of the most popular attractions in San Francisco, featuring classic elements such as an arched drum bridge, pagodas, stone lanterns, stepping stone paths, native Japanese plants, serene koi ponds, and a zen garden. Cherry blossom trees bloom throughout the garden in March and April.
Admission to the Japanese Tea Garden is free for San Francisco residents with valid ID. Free hours for everyone (even non-residents) are 9-10 am every Monday, Wednesday and Friday.

Please note that hours and costs change frequently.

events.title: Yerba Buena Illuminated: Free 95-Ft Art Projection on Market Street
events.description:
Yerba Buena Illuminated: Free 95-Ft Art Projection on Market Street
Yerba Buena Partnership
San Francisco has officially turned a downtown building into a giant art projector.

Yerba Buena Illuminated launched Tuesday, August 25, 2026 projecting giant digital artworks onto the historic Humboldt Bank Building at 785 Market St., at the top of Yerba Buena Lane. The massive projection covers a 95-foot-high by 46-foot-wide section of the building, turning one of Market Street’s historic facades into a giant outdoor art screen.

The free outdoor art show runs nightly from twilight until 10 p.m., with the first artwork on view for about 90 days. The inaugural projection is Jennifer Steinkamp’s It’s a nice day for a white wedding. (2008), from SFMOMA’s collection. Inspired by Billy Idol’s “White Wedding,” the digital artwork covers the Beaux-Arts-style building with a cascade of animated red, white and yellow wedding flowers.

The project is a collaboration between Yerba Buena Partnership, SFMOMA, the Museum of the African Diaspora and Yerba Buena Center for the Arts. And this first installation is just the beginning: MoAD and YBCA will curate future projections in 2027, so the giant building-as-canvas is sticking around.
The projection is designed to serve as a giant welcome sign for the Yerba Buena arts district, home to more than 60 public artworks and some of San Francisco’s biggest cultural institutions. The rotating projections will continue to light up the Humboldt Bank Buildi...

Submitted by the Event OrganizerInvisible Atlas — From Hiroshima and Nagasaki to Fukushima: The Invisible Threat of Nuclear Contamination
October 23–25, 2026 | Dance Mission Theater, San Francisco
Invisible Atlas, is a powerful multimedia dance performance exploring the invisible dangers of nuclear contamination and their lasting impact on humanity and the environment.

Inspired by the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the Fukushima nuclear meltdown, and ongoing concerns about radioactive waste in the San Francisco Bay Area, this performance connects historical tragedies with environmental challenges we face today.
Combining Butoh, contemporary dance, poetry, theatrical performance, immersive film projections, and live Japanese Shakuhachi and Taiko music, Invisible Atlas creates an emotionally compelling theatrical experience.
Through movement, sound, and visual storytelling, the performance invites audiences to reflect on the invisible consequences of nuclear history, our shared responsibility, and the future we want to create.

events.title: American Bread History Talk, Tasting & Guided Tour
events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerAndrew CoePlease join us on Saturday, October 24, 2026 for an extraordinary in-person opportunity to hear Andrew Coe speak about the history of American bread, while sampling a variety of historically important breads.
Why did supermarket white become America’s dominant bread, and how did rustic old-world bagels, ryes, and rolls find their way into our kitchens? Who was the early nineteenth-century dietary reformer who started the whole-grain revolution? Why not knead? An enriching and enlightening cultural chronicle, Andrew Coe answers these questions and more and offers carefully sourced historical recipes to inspire the home baker.

Note that this is not our usual 4th Sunday meeting date, it will be at 11:00. a.m on the 4th SATURDAY of the month.
The in-person presentation will take place at the historic City College, Culinary Arts building in San Francisco and will include a guided tour of the facility after the lecture and tasting. It is easily accessible by BART, a short walk from the Balboa Park station. Parking and building directions instructions will be sent a few days before the event.
Andrew Coe is an independent scholar and writer of many books including, Pirate’s Gold: A Gilded Age Saga of Family, Money and (Maybe) Murder, and along with his wife, Jane Ziegelman, co-authors of A Square Meal: A Culinary History of the Great Depression, which won a James Beard award. events.title: PBS/Frontlines One In A Million Documentary with Q&A
events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerCourtesy of PBS/FrontlinePost-screening Q&A with director Jack MacInnes & film subject, Israa moderated by Deborah Kaufman.
Filmed over ten years, One In A Million follows Israa from childhood to adulthood on an extraordinary journey from Syria to Germany — and back again. We first meet her at age 11 as she and her family are preparing to cross the Aegean Sea, risking everything in search of safety and a better life in Europe. What unfolds is a deeply personal chronicle of war, exile and heartbreak, as Israa grows up navigating adolescence, identity and belonging far from the home she was forced to leave. As Israa settles into life in Germany, new freedoms collide with the stabilizing pull of Syrian traditions, testing bonds and reshaping her sense of self.

Co-directed by Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes, the film bears witness to the remarkable trust between filmmakers and family, following Israa and her loved ones across borders, cultures and shifting circumstances. An intimate and nuanced coming-of-age story, One In A Million illuminates the complexities of the refugee experience while asking a universal question: what does it truly mean to call a place home?

events.title: When Manilatown Swung: The Manila Serenaders
events.description:
Manilatown Heritage FoundationWHEN MANILATOWN SWUNG: THE MANILA SERENADERS
What did Manilatown sound like when Kearny Street was alive with music?
Step into the sounds and stories of historic Manilatown for a special Club Mandalay: Music, Memory & Manilatown gathering featuring live jazz, archival photographs, family memories, and community Talk Story at the International Hotel Manilatown Center.

At the heart of the afternoon is Canuto Salaver, a drummer with the Manila Serenaders whose life was deeply connected to historic Manilatown and the I-Hotel. Members of the Salaver Family join guest interviewer Sabrina Oliveros to share family stories passed down about Canuto-his life around Kearny Street, his connection to the Bataan Cafe and Poolhall, and his years making music with the Manila Serenaders.
The musical lineage continues with Raymond Bambao, bassist with today’s Manilatown Jazz Ensemble, whose grandfather and grand-uncles also played with the Manila Serenaders.
Throughout the afternoon, the Manilatown Jazz Ensemble brings these histories back into sound with live musical interludes inspired by the era, while photographs and materials from the Manilatown Archives and family collections bring the world of historic Manilatown into view.
Audience members will also be invited into the Talk Story-because the memories carried by our families and communities are part of how history lives.
And because history can be fun: Feeling festive? Come dressed in your 1930s-40s finest!...

The Japanese YWCA building, at which this performance takes place, is a testament to the power of everyday people to enact change.
Join us for a multimedia performance incorporating taiko drumming, contemporary dance, jazz, poetry, and narration.

In Their Footsteps is directed by Melody Takata and features San Francisco Poet Laureate Genny Lim, jazz musicians Francis Wong and Lewis Jordan, dancer Hien Huynh, actor Suz Takeda, and youth and adult taiko drummers from GenRyu Arts.

events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerChabot StaffHalloween Hike!
Adults 21+, $40, Members receive $15 off
Immersive Trek

As the sun dips below the horizon and shadows stretch through the forest, the Halloween Hike begins! Join us for a moderate, 75–90 minute spine-tingling adventure through the darkened trails of the majestic Oakland Redwood forest, where ghostly tales and eerie surprises await.

World of Dumplings returns Sunday, October 25, with 25+ restaurant vendors serving up dumplings from around the globe, and admission is free.

events.description:
Jason EcklA $5 music festival in Napa? That’s right!
Not Loud Concerts presents the Napa $5 Folk Festival on Oct 25 from 2 – 5 pm.
This is a festival like no other – 9 bands, 3 stages, all indoors in downtown Napa, and all not too loud! Stroll between the stages hearing amazing internationally touring bands, local favorites, and a few surprises. Presented by Not Loud Concerts, this event takes out all of the hassles and discomfort of modern music festivals and puts the audience and musician’s comfort first. Best of all, admission is only $5.

The festival is held entirely indoors in the historic Native Sons of the Gold West (on Coombs), in multiple rooms on a couple of different floors. Large bands will be featured in the grand ballroom, acoustic-based bands will perform intimate sets in the wood paneled meeting room, and in the dance room there will be folk dancing lessons and some surprise acts.
Indoor bathrooms, chairs to sit in, room to dance and, of course, sound reinforcement that is not too loud make this festival one of a kind. All of this for just $5.
There is lots of nearby, free, parking and there are elevators in the hall, along with chairs in every room. The friendly folks at the Native Sons Hall will have drinks for sale.
Buying tickets in advance is recommended (and appreciated), but tickets will also be for sale at the door.

events.title: PBS/Frontlines One In A Million Documentary with Q&A
events.venue: Christopher B. Smith Rafael Film Center
events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerCourtesy of PBS/FrontlinePost-screening Q&A with director Jack MacInnes & film subject, Israa moderated by Diane Quon.
Filmed over ten years, One In A Million follows Israa from childhood to adulthood on an extraordinary journey from Syria to Germany — and back again. We first meet her at age 11 as she and her family are preparing to cross the Aegean Sea, risking everything in search of safety and a better life in Europe. What unfolds is a deeply personal chronicle of war, exile and heartbreak, as Israa grows up navigating adolescence, identity and belonging far from the home she was forced to leave. As Israa settles into life in Germany, new freedoms collide with the stabilizing pull of Syrian traditions, testing bonds and reshaping her sense of self.

Co-directed by Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes, the film bears witness to the remarkable trust between filmmakers and family, following Israa and her loved ones across borders, cultures and shifting circumstances. An intimate and nuanced coming-of-age story, One In A Million illuminates the complexities of the refugee experience while asking a universal question: what does it truly mean to call a place home?

events.title: Author Talk: How to Look Away with Daniel Peña and Sasha Vasilyuk
events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerPhoto courtesy of the authorIn How to Look Away, Daniel Peña explores how fringe elements of his Texas childhood—AM radio, conspiracy theories, Post-Cold War paranoia—came to dominate the American political discourse and contributed to our extreme tolerance of human rights abuses against migrants from Latin America and elsewhere. He asks: What compels us to look away from these abuses? And how do we wake ourselves into action?
These evocative essays braid journalism, cultural criticism, and memoir, roaming from the vestigial Comanche War battlefields of his native Austin, to the black markets of Mexico City, to the home of a cartel hitman’s family doomed to live in the unglamorous aftermath of his crimes. Writing from both Mexico and the United States, Daniel Peña reflects on two childhood fears: demons and the death penalty. Or the answer to the question, “Do you ever really belong to yourself?” A question that serves as the looking glass through which Peña meditates on American citizenship and the kinds of people we are willing to disappear in the name of the American project.

Daniel Peña is a Pushcart Prize-winning writer and Associate Professor at the University of North Texas where he teaches in the PhD Program in Creative Writing. Formerly, he was based out of the UNAM in Mexico City where he worked as Fulbright-Garcia Robles Scholar. Submitted by the Event OrganizerLenny GonzalezFilipino-American guitarist/composer Karl Evangelista presents an evening of daring, contemporary compositions, experimental sounds, and jazz-inflected improvisations, joined by Oakland-based AAPI trio Grex. The group performs selections from Grex’s “Auntie + Tebs,” a brand new album focused on revolutionary action in the Philippines and South Africa.
Karl Evangelista ranks among the vanguard of musicians pushing the traditions of jazz and experimental music into the future. Signal to Noise magazine hails Evangelista as “one of the most original instrumentalists and composers of his generation,” and as the creative force behind boundary-breaking group Grex, Evangelista’s music has been called “essential current-and-future listening” (Tiny Mix Tapes). Evangelista has explored new realms in sound and intercultural collaboration alongside the likes
of Andrew Cyrille, Fred Frith, Louis Moholo-Moholo, Trevor Watts, Bobby Bradford, Alexander Hawkins, Tatsu Aoki, and Asian Improv aRts co-founder Francis Wong.

Grex is an experimental/art rock band based out of Oakland, California. In biological terms, a “grex” is an entity composed of several smaller organisms. Grex (the band) explores the meeting point between surreal songcraft and the dark outer reaches of free jazz and industrial hip-hop.
The group has been called an “otherworldly experience” (Eugene Weekly) and “true genre warping music” (KFJC), recalling at turns the ecstatic energy...

events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerBota Tapas and Paella BarEvery Tuesday, Bota Tapas and Paella Bar near Union Square on the corner of Geary and Taylor Street is offering all Tapas for 10% Off! Come have the best authentic Spanish food in San Francisco, tell your friends, celebrate a birthday with us, or just come alone to have a large paella with a delicious Ox Tail, Patatas, or a savory Secreto Iberico tapas to make all of your senses go wild. We import many of our ingredients from Spain, including our Octopus (Pulpo), Sausage, Pork, and our rice.
So, don’t miss out and we look forward to making your dining experience a total success!

About Bota Tapas and Paella Bar
As an age-old tradition dating back to the early 1800s, Spanish travelers used “BOTA”, or traditional sheep-skinned repositories, to transport and share their wine. The Spaniards historically thrived on the values of sharing and community: two ideals that have buoyantly withstood the test of time. Tailored around these same ideals are Spain’s cuisine and the development of “tapas,” style dining – where individuals share small plates and memories. From Seville to San Francisco, and across the world, our goal is to initiate more memories – this is why and how we operate.

events.title: The Kabbalah of Meaning
events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerRabbi DovidJewish Wisdom for a Life That Matters
No matter how much we achieve, something within us still asks: “Is this it? Isn’t there something more?”

The Kabbalah of Meaning is a new six-session JLI course exploring the Jewish answer to that question. What are we really searching for—and where can it be found?
Drawing on Kabbalah and centuries of Jewish wisdom, we’ll uncover the essential building blocks of a deeply meaningful life. We’ll explore how purpose can be found in our work, relationships, challenges, accomplishments, and even the ordinary routines that fill our days.
You don’t have to revamp your life. You don’t need to meditate on a mountaintop. You simply need a new lens through which to see the rich world of meaning already woven into every part of your life.
Thoughtful, practical, and surprisingly relevant, this course offers fresh perspectives and useful tools for living with greater clarity, connection, and intention.
Try 1st class free.
No previous Jewish learning required. Come as you are—and bring your questions.

events.title: One City One Book: Cities as Ancestors (SF Main Library)
events.venue: San Francisco Main Library, Koret Auditorium
events.description:
San Francisco Public LibraryExplore how our relationships with cities, parks and the more-than-human world can shape our future. Inspired by Susanna Kwan’s Awake in the Floating City, the 2026 One City One Book selection, this conversation brings together local community leaders working on place-based environmental justice to consider what it means to be an ancestor and how the places we inhabit become part of our collective legacy.
Drawing on five years of the Parks as Ancestors series, inspired by the book, What Kind of Ancestor Do You Want to Be?, the discussion expands the conversation beyond protected parklands to consider urban spaces as living legacies.
This interactive program invites participants to consider what we inherit from the places and people who came before us-and what we will leave behind for those who come after. Attendees are welcome to bring a photograph or a sentimental object honoring someone they have lost, if they wish to incorporate it into the program.

Presented by San Francisco Public Library

events.title: PBS Film Preview: Lynn Novick’s “Crime and Punishment in America”
events.venue: Commonwealth Club World Affairs - Taube Family Auditorium
events.description: Submitted by the Event OrganizerCrime and Punishment in AmericaHow did the United States become the world’s leading incarcerator? Join acclaimed filmmaker Lynn Novick for a preview of her forthcoming PBS documentary, Crime and Punishment in America, executive produced by Ken Burns. She’ll join the film’s consulting producer Rahsaan Thomas, former co-host of the Peabody Award-winning podcast Ear Hustle and Executive Director of Empowerment Avenue, alongside correctional wellness advocate Stephen B. Walker and survivor advocate Jess Nichol, for a compelling conversation on the four-century history of criminal justice in America, and how Americans have wrestled with the problem of crime, the purpose of punishment and the meaning of justice. Much like the series, this conversation will feature differing perspectives from people who have been part of this imperfect system which continues to influence nearly all parts of our society.

events.title: Becoming Leaderful: A Panel Discussion on Building the Communities We Want
events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerOakland Asian Cultural CenterJoin a discussion among local activists and leaders on how to unlock and amplify our capabilities in a moment which calls for leadership from every community member. As our community and our structures come under attack, this is the time for deep reflection and action, to ask ourselves who we are, who we can be, and how to become the people we have been waiting for. Our panelists will share their processes of refuting the model minority myth, our own learned powerlessness, and what it looks like to take an active part in ongoing social change. Attendees will leave the session with new models and inspiration to build lasting change in their communities.
The panelists are Claudia Leung from New Breath, Tash Nguyen from Restore Oakland, and Krishna Desai, Esq. of Desai Tran, with moderator Kim Tran.

About the Panelists

Claudia Leung (she/they) is a queer, disabled, mixed-race second-generation Chinese American born and raised in the Bay Area. At New Breath Foundation, she serves as the Director of Programs, leading in strategic grantmaking, capacity building, evaluation, and learning. Throughout her career, Claudia has consistently focused on centering marginalized communities to effect intersectional cultural and social change. events.description:
Japanese Tea Garden’s Free Admission Hour (Golden Gate Park)
Japanese Tea Garden
The Japanese Tea Garden provides visitors from around the world with an opportunity to experience the natural beauty, tranquility, and harmony of a Japanese-style garden in the heart of San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park.
Originally created as a “Japanese Village” exhibit for the 1894 California Midwinter International Exposition, the Japanese Tea Garden endures as one of the most popular attractions in San Francisco, featuring classic elements such as an arched drum bridge, pagodas, stone lanterns, stepping stone paths, native Japanese plants, serene koi ponds, and a zen garden. Cherry blossom trees bloom throughout the garden in March and April.
Admission to the Japanese Tea Garden is free for San Francisco residents with valid ID. Free hours for everyone (even non-residents) are 9-10 am every Monday, Wednesday and Friday.

Please note that hours and costs change frequently.

A Mission Bernal Tasting takes you from Cortland Avenue to 29th Street with a taste waiting at every stop: Nepali, Persian, Nicaraguan, Mexican, Chinese, Japanese, Greek, Indian and Italian, plus local pizza, beer, cider and Thai tea. Ten countries in four blocks, and more than twenty restaurants and bars taking part.
One ticket covers the whole route. You walk at your own pace, in any order, from 5 to 8 pm. Check in any time from 5 pm at The Front Porch, 65 29th Street, and pick up a map.

This is a neighborhood fundraiser, not a promoter’s event. Every dollar goes to a permanent mosaic by Colette Crutcher, the artist behind the 16th Avenue Tiled Steps, on the long-tagged retaining walls at Cortland and Prospect. More than 120 neighbors made tiles for it by hand at free workshops, and a row of tiles along the base of the mural portrays the small businesses of both corridors.
The two previous Taste of Bernal events on Cortland Avenue sold out at 300 tickets. This is the first one on Mission Street.
Tickets: $65 general admission, $40 for young people and seasoned adults. Wear comfortable shoes and come hungry.

events.title: Author Talk: Parini Shroff with Tanya Žilinskas
events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerPhoto courtesy of the authorParini Shroff, bestselling author of The Bandit Queens, presents her newest novel, Some People in this special conversation with Tanya Žilinskas at the Mill Valley Library.
A man on the brink of divorce is forced to care for his injured future-ex-mother-in-law in this wise, witty, and heartfelt novel.

Malti Patel is absolutely fine. Concussed and bruised, maybe, but fine. Certainly fine enough to not need her daughter’s soon-to-be-ex-husband, Nathan Whitlock, playing nurse in her home while she recuperates. And yet, that’s exactly the quandary in which she finds herself. Her doctor insists on in-home supervision for seven days, and with her daughter, Kavya, abroad at grad school in India, Nathan proves too much of a do-gooder to let Malti rehabilitate alone. Seven days of Nathan, the man divorcing her daughter for all manner of reasons: cultural misunderstanding, emotional walls, simmering hostility…most of them having to do with Kavya’s baggage from her childhood.
Rich with emotional depth, Some People paints a nuanced portrait of love, forgiveness, and our timeless quest for understanding and acceptance.
Parini Shroff is the bestselling author of The Bandit Queens, which was a Good Morning America Buzz Pick, a PEN Open Book finalist, and longlisted for the Andrew Carnegie Medal and the Women’s Prize for Fiction. events.title: Astronomy on Tap San Francisco
events.description:
AoT SF

Local astronomers talking about stars, planets, and the universe at your neighborhood bar. No PhD required.

NOTE: We are at Public Works this month, with more space for everyone! The event is still free, but the venue will ask you to fulfill the 1 drink minimum by buying a $12 drink ticket.
Astronomy on Tap is is a free public lecture series where astronomers give short, laid-back talks over drinks at local bars. No background in science required — our scientists share cool stuff about space while the audience sits back and relaxes, with plenty of time to indulge their curiosity and ask whatever questions they want.

This month, we’re hosting:
Nick Rodd (LBL) – The Latest in the Search for Dark Matter
and
Seth Shostak (SETI Institute) – Are We Alone in the Universe?
Rodd is a Divisional Fellow at Lawrence Berkeley Lab and former faculty member at CERN. Shostak is the senior astronomer for the SETI Institute, co-hosts of the weekly podcast Big Picture Science, and author of four books on the search for extraterrestrial life.
Astronomy on Tap takes place in cities all over the world. This is a revival of the San Francisco chapter, which regularly hosted events before the pandemic. We’re excited to be back on a monthly basis!
The event is free, but there is a 1 drink minimum. Food (by jeong.sf) will be available with vegetarian options.
If you’d like to join our mailing list to hear about future events, sign up here.

events.title: Opening Night Echoes of the Past: Nature as Metaphor
events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerFrancophone MuseumThe Francophone Museum is pleased to present Echoes of the Past: Nature as Metaphor, a new exhibition by award-winning San Francisco artist Danièle Erville, with a special opening night reception on October 29th.
Landscapes have always been at the heart of Danièle’s work, whether painted en plein air or imagined from within. Inspired by Jules Supervielle’s poem “Le petit bois,” the show brings together drawing, painting, and collage that use trees and landscapes as metaphors for memory and feeling. Each piece is a direct expression of Danièle’s interiority at the moment of creation, and together they show how the things that move us as children can speak to us for a lifetime.

Danièle Erville holds a BA from Clark University, studied at the Maryland Institute College of Art, and graduated from the School of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. Her work is part of the Photograph Study Collection at the Smithsonian American Art Museum and has been exhibited in France, Boston, Santa Fe, and throughout the Bay Area. See her work on Instagram @danieleervilleart.
Join us for the opening of the exhibition: meet the artist, enjoy light refreshments, and be among the first to see the show.

Heartbroken Michael comes to Berlin to return his ex-girlfriend’s keys and ends up trapped in her apartment building during a zombie outbreak. This was Germany’s very first zombie film.

events.title: Japanese Woodblock Prints & the Language of Flowers: Gallery Talk
events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerArt House SFIn 2015, Japan’s Empress Michiko chose a gold-leaf cherry-blossom woodblock print by Yowsaku Sekino for the Imperial Palace. Now 20 of Sekino’s prints are on view at Art House SF in the Castro, in what are his only solo exhibitions outside Japan.
Gallery founder Max Khusid leads a small-group talk standing at the prints:

Ukiyo-e, shin-hanga and sōsaku-hanga: three ways Japan made woodblock prints
How Japanese prints reached Van Gogh and, later, Steve Jobs
How Sekino layers 10+ hand-carved blocks and applies gold leaf by hand
Hanakotoba, the Japanese language of flowers: what each bloom on the wall is saying

Limited to 15 people. Tickets are $10, credited toward any purchase. The exhibition itself is free and open Wednesday to Sunday through November 1.

For more than 35 years, Los Cenzontles has empowered generations of young people through music, dance, and storytelling while preserving and celebrating Mexican and Mexican American cultural traditions. Directed by Bay Area filmmaker James Hall, the film weaves together decades of archival footage, intimate interviews, and performances that showcase the organization’s lasting impact on artists and communities alike. The documentary also features appearances by cultural icons including Linda Ronstadt, Los Lobos, Lalo Guerrero, Taj Mahal, Jackson Browne, Ry Cooder, Flaco Jiménez, and more.

A special live performance by Los Cenzotles will kick off the screening.

Japanese Tea Garden
The Japanese Tea Garden provides visitors from around the world with an opportunity to experience the natural beauty, tranquility, and harmony of a Japanese-style garden in the heart of San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park.
Originally created as a “Japanese Village” exhibit for the 1894 California Midwinter International Exposition, the Japanese Tea Garden endures as one of the most popular attractions in San Francisco, featuring classic elements such as an arched drum bridge, pagodas, stone lanterns, stepping stone paths, native Japanese plants, serene koi ponds, and a zen garden. Cherry blossom trees bloom throughout the garden in March and April.
Admission to the Japanese Tea Garden is free for San Francisco residents with valid ID. Free hours for everyone (even non-residents) are 9-10 am every Monday, Wednesday and Friday.

events.title: “Another Lamp Show” 100+ One-Of-A-Kind Art Lamps
events.description: Kelly IshikawaOpening October 30th, 500 Capp Street Foundation presents Another Lamp Show, a fundraiser in support of the historic David Ireland House in San Francisco’s Mission District. Co-organized with artist and union electrician Rico Duenas, the fundraiser invites more than 100 artists, including Chelsea Ryoko Wong, StudioAhead, Sahar Khoury, Mike Arcega, Roman de Salvo, Dana Hemenway, and David Horvitz, to reinterpret the lamp as Ireland himself once did: as a vehicle for sculptural invention. Through salvaged materials, experimentation, and playful humor, these artists have made one-of-a-kind functioning lamps that will be for sale in person at 500 Capp Street and online during the fundraiser. Throughout his home at 500 Capp Street, Ireland’s idiosyncratic lamps set the tone for the space. In the parlor rooms, Ireland replaced an upstairs chandelier with a suspended light fixture composed of wire and blowtorches, which when lit creates a precarious and entrancing “Fire Drawing” that reflects off the home’s high-gloss surfaces. Other oddly utilitarian lamps made by Ireland, often of concrete and copper piping, are functional pieces of art that continue to illuminate the exhibitions on display today. “Another Lamp Show brings together so much of what we value at 500 Capp Street: art in everyday life, experimentation, and artists sharing knowledge with one another. We’re especially thankful to Rico Duenas, who is co-organizing the exhibition and brings his experience as...

Wear your costumes and have a spooky time
Mermaid Island has been brewing chaos in the underground LA punk scene since fall of 2022. Founded by Canadian vocalist, guitarist, and songwriter Alex MacDonald, the band quickly became known for their high-octane performances. Based on building and protecting the DIY community, Mermaid Island is about connecting with each other in real life, and creating more space for charged, purposeful aggression.
“It was always about the shows. We have as much fun playing for no one in our lockout as we do for a packed crowd.” says MacDonald. The band solidified their presence in the LA scene before ever setting foot in a studio. They tracked most of their debut album live off the floor in two days, holding onto the same energy that keeps their shows magnetic. Mermaid Island is creating a space where people feel inspired to pick up their own instruments. “We just want to play shows with our friends so we can remember what joy feels like on this shit show planet.”

events.title: Yerba Buena Illuminated: Free 95-Ft Art Projection on Market Street
events.description:
Yerba Buena Illuminated: Free 95-Ft Art Projection on Market Street
Yerba Buena Partnership
San Francisco has officially turned a downtown building into a giant art projector.

Yerba Buena Illuminated launched Tuesday, August 25, 2026 projecting giant digital artworks onto the historic Humboldt Bank Building at 785 Market St., at the top of Yerba Buena Lane. The massive projection covers a 95-foot-high by 46-foot-wide section of the building, turning one of Market Street’s historic facades into a giant outdoor art screen.

The free outdoor art show runs nightly from twilight until 10 p.m., with the first artwork on view for about 90 days. The inaugural projection is Jennifer Steinkamp’s It’s a nice day for a white wedding. (2008), from SFMOMA’s collection. Inspired by Billy Idol’s “White Wedding,” the digital artwork covers the Beaux-Arts-style building with a cascade of animated red, white and yellow wedding flowers.

The project is a collaboration between Yerba Buena Partnership, SFMOMA, the Museum of the African Diaspora and Yerba Buena Center for the Arts. And this first installation is just the beginning: MoAD and YBCA will curate future projections in 2027, so the giant building-as-canvas is sticking around.
The projection is designed to serve as a giant welcome sign for the Yerba Buena arts district, home to more than 60 public artworks and some of San Francisco’s biggest cultural institutions. The rotating projections will continue to light up the Humboldt Bank Buildi...

events.title: Pigeons Playing Ping Pong
events.description: Submitted by the Event OrganizerThe UC TheatreFor Pigeons Playing Ping Pong, music is a living flame—one demanding relentless tending, fresh kindling, and the collective breath of community to sustain it. On their eighth studio album, Feed The Fire (No Coincidence Records), the Baltimore quartet—“Scrambled Greg” Ormont [vocals, guitar], Jeremy Schon [guitar, vocals], Ben Carrey [bass, vocals], and Alex “Gator” Petropulos [drums, vocals]—push their psychedelic funk odyssey into its most expansive incarnation yet. Across sixteen years, eight albums, and countless sweat-soaked performances, Pigeons have mastered transformation, deepening their connection with their devoted fanbase and channeling life’s seismic shifts into fuel for their unquenchable fire. “The ‘fire’ represents our passion,” explains Ormont. “Making music feels like something we were born to do… Feed The Fire is the perfect metaphor for our unwavering commitment to keep evolving.” Significant milestones, from headlining major stages to their fan-centric Domefest, underscore their remarkable journey.

Japanese Tea Garden
The Japanese Tea Garden provides visitors from around the world with an opportunity to experience the natural beauty, tranquility, and harmony of a Japanese-style garden in the heart of San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park.
Originally created as a “Japanese Village” exhibit for the 1894 California Midwinter International Exposition, the Japanese Tea Garden endures as one of the most popular attractions in San Francisco, featuring classic elements such as an arched drum bridge, pagodas, stone lanterns, stepping stone paths, native Japanese plants, serene koi ponds, and a zen garden. Cherry blossom trees bloom throughout the garden in March and April.
Admission to the Japanese Tea Garden is free for San Francisco residents with valid ID. Free hours for everyone (even non-residents) are 9-10 am every Monday, Wednesday and Friday.

Japanese Tea Garden
The Japanese Tea Garden provides visitors from around the world with an opportunity to experience the natural beauty, tranquility, and harmony of a Japanese-style garden in the heart of San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park.
Originally created as a “Japanese Village” exhibit for the 1894 California Midwinter International Exposition, the Japanese Tea Garden endures as one of the most popular attractions in San Francisco, featuring classic elements such as an arched drum bridge, pagodas, stone lanterns, stepping stone paths, native Japanese plants, serene koi ponds, and a zen garden. Cherry blossom trees bloom throughout the garden in March and April.
Admission to the Japanese Tea Garden is free for San Francisco residents with valid ID. Free hours for everyone (even non-residents) are 9-10 am every Monday, Wednesday and Friday.

events.title: Free Behind-the-Scenes Talk: How SF Neo-Futurists Run 100 Shows a Year (SF Main Library)
events.venue: SFPL Main Library Steve Silver Room (4th Floor)
events.description:
SF Neo-FuturistsLearn what it takes to write, direct and perform 100 SHOWS A YEAR as a small group of artists who also RUN THE BUSINESS together. It’s not a sitcom, it’s The San Francisco Neo-Futurists. They put on the Infinite Wrench, the show the SF Chronicle calls one of “22 San Francisco things everyone must do!”
They’ll pull back the curtain on how they operate as a non-hierarchical consensus-based collective to organize performance space, run committees, budget and raise funds and ultimately put on a show every week. They’ll also cover their process for writing new material for a new cast of performers to put on a different show every Friday and Saturday night.
The SF Neos are a collective of wildly prolific artists dedicated to the perpetual creation of experimental theatre that is immediate, ephemeral, accessible and cheap. They believe the stage is an extension of daily life: they perform as themselves in a non-illusory, interactive style that challenges the audience to create alongside them as active participants with a voice of their own. They respect and uplift each other on and off stage through non-hierarchical accountability, collective decision-making and anti-oppression practice of all kinds.

Japanese Tea Garden
The Japanese Tea Garden provides visitors from around the world with an opportunity to experience the natural beauty, tranquility, and harmony of a Japanese-style garden in the heart of San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park.
Originally created as a “Japanese Village” exhibit for the 1894 California Midwinter International Exposition, the Japanese Tea Garden endures as one of the most popular attractions in San Francisco, featuring classic elements such as an arched drum bridge, pagodas, stone lanterns, stepping stone paths, native Japanese plants, serene koi ponds, and a zen garden. Cherry blossom trees bloom throughout the garden in March and April.
Admission to the Japanese Tea Garden is free for San Francisco residents with valid ID. Free hours for everyone (even non-residents) are 9-10 am every Monday, Wednesday and Friday.

photo from the showMarin Arts & Crafts Show returns to the Marin Center Exhibit Hall November 6–8, filling the hall with more than 200 exhibits of fine craft, art and artisan goods. Arriving just as the holiday season gets underway, the three-day market brings together an exciting mix of artists, artisans and craftspeople for a weekend of art, handcraft and seasonal discoveries.
Inspired by the Arts & Crafts movement, the show celebrates craftsmanship, thoughtful design and artistic expression in its many forms. Visitors will find jewelry, ceramics, textiles, glass, woodwork, fine art, furniture, wearable art and specialty foods from artisan food makers. From hand-dyed silks and sculptural ceramics to finely crafted jewelry and heirloom-quality woodworking, the market brings together traditional techniques, fresh ideas and contemporary design.
Throughout the weekend, visitors can talk with artists about their work, watch demonstrations and explore the many forms of handcraft represented at the show. It’s a chance to see the details up close, hear how things are made and get to know some of the people behind the work.

The November show brings a festive atmosphere to the Marin Center, with a bustling marketplace of fine crafts, art and artisan foods. events.title: Free “Ocean Beach” Photo Exhibit: 24 Bay Area Photographers
events.description:
Featured photo by Sachi CunninghamHeavy Water Collective Presents: Ocean Beach brings together 24 photographers who turn their lenses toward the Pacific, finding pockets of magic amidst a vast liquid field of chaos.

Some of these works play with the juxtaposition of ocean wilderness and concrete cityscapes, framing surfers speeding down powerful waves with electrical wiring and concrete in the foreground. Others ask you to forget the city and immerse in how light, energy, and human shapes can dance together. Each photograph displays a single permutation within an infinite, ever-changing landscape.

We invite you to share the awe and appreciation we have for this beach and enjoy taking in a different dimension of San Francisco.

events.title: ZooLights at San Francisco Zoo (Nov. 6-Jan 3)
events.description:
San Francisco Zoo & GardensSan Francisco Zoo & Gardens is thrilled to announce its all-new, two-month-long ZooLights evening holiday program that will light up the Zoo in spectacular fashion from November 6 through January 3, 2027. The nighttime event represents the return of ZooLights, which the Zoo last hosted in 2018.

“The Zoo is the perfect venue for a safe, outdoor holiday lights experience,” said Cassandra Costello, CEO and Executive Director. “We have taken this event to the next level, creating 14 dazzling zones, with winter, botanical or animal-themed components. It’s going to be truly breathtaking, and a great experience for the entire family.”

In addition to traditional holiday zones, where guests will walk through awe-inspiring lighted tunnels and stroll among giant candy canes, giant ornaments and gift boxes, there’s an entire frozen zone, with 10-foot-tall icicles, sparkling snowflakes, a frozen forest, a massive ice throne and frozen sleigh for that perfect family photo.

“The effect will be magical,” said Costello. “Overall, ZooLights will have more than one million lights, and the walk-through areas include amazing photo ops, and nods to the City of San Francisco with a Golden Gate Bridge and the iconic cable car.”

Whimsical animal shapes and scenes will dot the landscape, using 2D and 3D illuminations of a rhino and gorilla, even a tree full of ring-tailed lemurs. Vibrantly colored, larger-than-life butterflies are part of an enchanting botanical pathway,...

events.venue: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA)
events.description:
Manilatown Heritage Foundation“Two Films. One Manilatown Legacy.” brings two generations of San Francisco’s Manilatown and International Hotel history to the big screen at SFMOMA for a special FREE double-feature presentation.
At 1 PM, experience the San Francisco premiere of the newly enhanced and restored edition of Curtis Choy’s landmark 1983 documentary, “The Fall of the I-Hotel”. The film chronicles the decade-long struggle to save San Francisco’s International Hotel and the August 4, 1977 eviction of its predominantly Filipino and Chinese elder tenants. Following the screening, filmmaker Curtis Choy joins co-producers of the enhanced edition for a community conversation moderated by Caroline Ocampo.
At 3 PM, experience the premiere of “Manilatown Manang”, the story of Jeanette Gandionco Lazam-artist, activist, and one of the few women who lived in the International Hotel as a Tenant Defender during the historic anti-eviction movement. The film follows Jeanette’s journey from the I-Hotel struggle through a lifetime of activism, art, and community. Following the premiere, Jeanette Lazam joins the film’s producers and creative team for a community conversation moderated by Caroline Ocampo.

Together, the films create a powerful dialogue between past and present: audiences first encounter Jeanette as a young activist in Choy’s historic documentary, then experience the continuation of her story in Manilatown Manang.

events.title: Free “Wood Street” Film Screening on Oakland’s Unhoused + Q&A (SF Main Library)
events.description:
Caron CreightonWOOD STREET follows a year in the life of Oakland’s largest unhoused encampment as its residents face an imminent eviction that threatens to dismantle their community. As notices appear and police move in, residents organize — building barricades, filing lawsuits, and protesting at City Hall to fight for their right to stay. Told through immersive verité, the film places viewers inside the encampment, capturing the urgency, resilience, and emotional toll of collective resistance. At its center are John and LaMonté, whose bond is tested as pressure mounts — LaMonté’s mental health deteriorates while John struggles to remain sober. When the eviction comes, the community is physically erased, but its spirit endures.
The film will be followed by a Q&A with the film team, members of the Wood Street community and the editor of Street Sheet newspaper.

events.title: Free Night Walking Tour of Chinatown Alleyways + North Beach
events.address: Bush Street &, Grant Ave, San Francisco, CA 94108
events.description:
Filip ToddAfter dark, Chinatown quiets down. That’s when this walk starts.
It’s a free 90-minute evening tour that begins at the Dragon Gate and works up through Chinatown’s back alleys to the point where the neighbourhood turns into North Beach. Along the way: the old tong buildings on Waverly Place, the gambling alleyways, a Bruce Lee mural, Jack Kerouac Alley and City Lights Bookstore. It ends at Golden Boy Pizza.
Two neighbourhoods pressed up against each other for more than a century, and the seam between them is the most interesting part of either.

The tour is free in the real sense — no ticket, nothing paid up front. At the end you decide what it was worth, and there’s no obligation.
Guided in English. Meets at the Dragon Gate, corner of Bush Street and Grant Avenue.

events.title: Free Book Reading: A Childhood on the Hippie Trail at Adobe Books
events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerCaleb Dardick, authorIn 1970, five-year-old Caleb Dardick set off with his family on an extraordinary 20,000-mile journey from Amsterdam to India in a VW bus. His father used a wheelchair, his mother was living with undiagnosed bipolar disorder, and the three children found themselves immersed in the counterculture’s wild search for freedom and enlightenment.
Join Dardick at San Francisco’s Adobe Books for a free reading and discussion of his new memoir, The Adventures of Superfreak: My Childhood on the Hippie Trail (Running Wild Press, 2026).

The book is a child’s-eye view of the counterculture, filled with adventure, humor, wonder, and instability. As San Francisco approaches the 60th anniversary of the Summer of Love in 2027, Dardick offers an unusual perspective on that era: the children who were along for the ride.
A former San Francisco resident who spent nearly three decades in Berkeley, Dardick wrote much of the memoir in the Bay Area.
Saturday, November 7, 2026, 6–7:30 PM
Adobe Books, 3130 24th Street, San Francisco
Free admission. No RSVP required. Books available for purchase and signing.

events.description:
Japanese Tea Garden’s Free Admission Hour (Golden Gate Park)
Japanese Tea Garden
The Japanese Tea Garden provides visitors from around the world with an opportunity to experience the natural beauty, tranquility, and harmony of a Japanese-style garden in the heart of San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park.
Originally created as a “Japanese Village” exhibit for the 1894 California Midwinter International Exposition, the Japanese Tea Garden endures as one of the most popular attractions in San Francisco, featuring classic elements such as an arched drum bridge, pagodas, stone lanterns, stepping stone paths, native Japanese plants, serene koi ponds, and a zen garden. Cherry blossom trees bloom throughout the garden in March and April.
Admission to the Japanese Tea Garden is free for San Francisco residents with valid ID. Free hours for everyone (even non-residents) are 9-10 am every Monday, Wednesday and Friday.

events.title: Handel’s The Power of Music (Stanford)
events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerDennis BoltCan Music Change the Course of History?
Three centuries ago, George Frideric Handel explored a bold idea: that music can change how people think, feel, and act.

Music Director Peter Whelan and Philharmonia Baroque Orchestra & Chorale open the 2026/27 season with Handel’s The Power of Music, featuring Alexander’s Feast, a vocal and choral masterpiece inspired by a legendary banquet marking Alexander the Great’s victory over Persia. As the feast unfolds, poet-musician Timotheus uses music to influence the conqueror and change the course of history.
Bay Area audiences will be first in the U.S. to hear Handel’s 1742 Dublin version, performed on period instruments and in the style of the time.
Performances
Stanford: Wednesday, November 11 at 7:30 PM (Bing Hall)
San Francisco: Friday, November 13 at 7:30 PM (Herbst Theatre)

events.description:
San Francisco Trans Film FestivalNovember 12-14, screenings at 7pm-8pm and 9pm-10pm each night\
Sliding scale tickets for screenings start at $5 (plus $1.28 fee)
The San Francisco Transgender Film Festival (SFTFF) celebrates 29 years of innovative, experimental, and outside-the-box films by transgender and gender-nonconforming filmmakers.

Spanning 12-days from November 12-22 and comprised of seven short film programs showcasing 37 films, SFTFF 2026 will be a hybrid festival, presented both in person and online, and featuring a range of genres from documentaries and politics to animation, dance, music, romance, coming-of-age tales, and thrillers.
SFTFF will host in-person programs Nov. 12-14 at the Roxie Theater, 3117 16th St., SF and will offer on demand access to each of the programs through Nov. 22nd. Films are closed captioned for Deaf and hard-of-hearing audiences; tickets are $0-$50, sliding scale/donation-based, inclusive of fees.
Presented by San Francisco Trans Film Festival

On Thursday, November 12th at 7:30pm, you and yours can experience that magic right here in the heart of Hayes Valley in San Francisco!

events.title: Handel’s The Power of Music
events.address: 401 Van Ness Avenue, San Francisco, CA
events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerDennis BoltCan Music Change the Course of History?
Three centuries ago, George Frideric Handel explored a bold idea: that music can change how people think, feel, and act.

Music Director Peter Whelan and Philharmonia Baroque Orchestra & Chorale open the 2026/27 season with Handel’s The Power of Music, featuring Alexander’s Feast, a vocal and choral masterpiece inspired by a legendary banquet marking Alexander the Great’s victory over Persia. As the feast unfolds, poet-musician Timotheus uses music to influence the conqueror and change the course of history.
Bay Area audiences will be first in the U.S. to hear Handel’s 1742 Dublin version, performed on period instruments and in the style of the time.
Performances
Stanford: Wednesday, November 11 at 7:30 PM (Bing Hall)
San Francisco: Friday, November 13 at 7:30 PM (Herbst Theatre)
Berkeley: Saturday, November 14 at 2:30 PM (First Congregational Church)

events.description:
San Francisco Department of Children, Youth & Their Families (DCYF)

This is Your City. This is Your Voice. This is Your Future. Share your story about growing up and raising your family in San Francisco.

Every family has a story. Every voice matters. Please share yours.
Join us for the District 4 Sunset Family Summit! The This Is Your City: Family Summit Series invites families, caregivers, young people, and community members from across San Francisco to help shape the future of our city.

Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, 11:00 a.m. – 1:30 p.m.
Sunset Recreation Center, 2201 Lawton St, SF, CA 94122

Free food, childcare, and interpretation are provided. Please note all interpretation requests must be made 48 hours or more prior to the Family Summit.
Who should attend? Everyone is welcome. This event highlights District 4, but you can attend any Family Summit that fits your schedule.
Why are we gathering? The Family Summit Series is part of San Francisco’s first Citywide Community Needs Assessment. Through conversations with families across the city, we’re learning what matters most to children, youth, young adults, and families. What we learn will help improve future planning, programs, and services.
Whether you’ve lived in San Francisco your whole life or recently made it your home, your experiences and ideas matter.
District 4 Neighborhoods include: Central Sunset, Outer Sunset, Parkside, Pine Lake Park, Lakeshore, Merced Manor, and Farallon Islands

events.title: Echoes of the Seasons: A Piano Dialogue Between East and West
events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerSFPLExplore how Eastern and Western composers interpret the seasons across different musical traditions. Western selections express vivid natural imagery, from Vivaldi’s dynamic storms to Tchaikovsky’s romantic winter scenes and the reflective mood of Autumn Leaves. These works translate the physical world into sound through color, emotion and narrative.
Eastern musical philosophy centers Yijing (意境), an aesthetic that blends atmosphere, poetry and spiritual resonance. Rooted in the Chinese pentatonic scale, this approach moves beyond direct depiction, inviting listeners to experience nature as a contemplative reflection of the self.

Through classical masterworks, jazz and traditional Chinese repertoire, this lecture‑recital highlights how artistic languages encounter one another across cultures. The program invites audiences to hear how different musical philosophies interpret the seasons and how these perspectives generate deeper understanding of memory, place and expression.

events.title: Handel’s The Power of Music (Berkeley)
events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerDennis BoltCan Music Change the Course of History?
Three centuries ago, George Frideric Handel explored a bold idea: that music can change how people think, feel, and act.

Bay Area audiences will be first in the U.S. to hear Handel’s 1742 Dublin version, performed on period instruments and in the style of the time.

Fort Point Beer Co

A one-night celebration at Fort Point Valencia to honor our favorite fall tradition: the release of our Manzanita Smoked Altbier.

First 4-packs of the season: Sold to go before they’re available anywhere else.

events.title: Free 2026 Art Week Opening: Kinetic Sculpture Show “Abiogenesis” at SF’s Heron Arts
events.description:
Image courtesy of artists.Heron Arts is pleased to announce Abiogenesis, a duo exhibition featuring Philip Beesley and Casey Curran. The opening reception for Abiogenesis is Saturday, November 14th, 2026 from 6-9pm. It is free and open to the public and will be part of San Francisco Art Week. The exhibition will be on view to the public until January 24th, by appointment only.

Abiogenesis brings together the work of Philip Beesley and Casey Curran around an elusive phenomenon: the emergence of life from inert matter. Their work assembles unmistakably artificial elements that, in their cellular forms and gentle movement, begin to suggest life. Lacework becomes membrane. Scaffolds of repeating cells become skeletons of organisms. Glowing, shimmering light evokes the pulses of nature. Mechanical gestures appear to breathe, bloom, and reach into the world.

Intimations of life within Beesley’s and Curran’s sculptures suggest that living form can emerge from the matter of the earth. Beesley and Curran probe this threshold through myth, science, and sensitive sculptural expression.

Artist Bios

Philip Beesley is a Canadian artist whose sculptures explore the threshold between inert matter and living form. At the heart of his work are glowing, pulsing, precious structures composed of innumerable finely crafted elements. events.description:

Lindy in the Park
Get ready to swing in Golden Gate Park every sunny Sunday at “Lindy in the Park,” a weekly free event near the de Young Museum, when the streets of Golden Gate Park are closed to traffic and the dancers take over.
This in person event resumed June 20, 2021
Lindy in the Park | Free Outdoor Swing Dance & Lessons
Every Sunday | 11 am to 2 pm
JFK Dr. btwn 8th and 10th, behind the De Young Museum, Golden Gate Park, SF
FREE
Rain and Bay to Breakers cancels, but other than that, Lindy in the Park takes place every Sunday – even on holidays – so even if New Year’s Day, Christmas, or Fourth of July falls on a Sunday, they’ll be out there dancing. On the very rare occasion when they cancel, they’ll make a new posting on their website, usually by 10am on Sunday. Lindy in the Park’s Schedule FAQ

Free Beginners Swing Lessons | Noon to 12:30 pm
Lindy in the Park offers a free weekly beginning swing dance lesson, taught by Hep Jen. The lessons are short, easy and fun and then you can practice your new steps with the whole group until 2 pm.
No partner is required, as they rotate leaders and followers throughout the lesson.

events.title: SF’s Winter “Renegade Craft Fair” at Fort Mason (Nov. 14-15)
events.description:
SF’s Winter “Renegade Craft Fair” at Fort Mason (Nov. 14-15)
Renegrade Craft
Renegade San Francisco Winter Craft Fair 2026 returns to Fort Mason Center Festival Pavilion on November 14 + 15, 2026, for a weekend of holiday shopping featuring 250+ curated artists and independent small businesses.
Browse handmade gifts and creative finds, including ceramics, apparel, jewelry, home goods, accessories, art, and more. With independent makers from around the country, it’s a great spot to find something more original than the usual holiday gifts.
Admission is free, with a suggested $5 contribution payable via QR code onsite. Contributions support Renegade Craft’s mission to make its fairs accessible while helping independent artists and creative small businesses thrive.

Rain or shine: The fair is held indoors, with food trucks and additional features outdoors.
Food and drinks: Food trucks and other food and coffee options are available. You can also bring your own food and nonalcoholic beverages.
Accessibility: The Festival Pavilion is at ground level, with a wheelchair-accessible elevator to the mezzanine. Most of the fair and all restrooms are on the ground floor.
Getting there: Carpooling, rideshares, biking, and public transit are encouraged. On Sunday, November 15, Marina Boulevard will be closed from 6:30 am to 11:30 am, so expect alternate directions into Fort Mason and possible congestion.
Animals: Service animals are welcome.

events.title: “Free Oakland Up” Market: Shop for Free Treasures (Every Friday-Sunday)
events.description:
“Free Oakland Up” Market: Shop for Free Treasures (Every Friday-Sunday)
freeoaklandup
Free Oakland UP, a Social Practice Project by Jocelyn Meggait, is open Fridays through Sundays from 12–4 PM, offering free materials for art, collage, and junk journals such as ephemera, electronics parts, books, and household goods. Outdoor items are entirely free to take (just don’t take their tables, bins or shelves), while indoor visitors can choose one free item per person per day, with additional items available for a monetary donation. Some plants and select treasures are for sale. The shop aims to keep usable items out of the landfill.
Original Event Description:
_Free Oakland UP is open Friday to Sunday, 12-4, with new treasures and plants added weekly. Outside: everything is FREE, take as much as you want except my tables, bins and shelves. Loads of materials for collage, assemblage and junk journals: ephemera, typewriter and electronics parts, books, cds and DVDs, magazines, household goods, etc. Inside: ONE free item per person per day and for a fair monetary donation you may choose more. Plants and select treasures are for sale to help pay for rent and expenses. Thank you for keeping treasures out of the landfill._

events.address: 75 Hagiwara Tea Garden Dr, San Francisco, CA
events.description:
Japanese Tea Garden’s Free Admission Hour (Golden Gate Park)
Japanese Tea Garden
The Japanese Tea Garden provides visitors from around the world with an opportunity to experience the natural beauty, tranquility, and harmony of a Japanese-style garden in the heart of San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park.
Originally created as a “Japanese Village” exhibit for the 1894 California Midwinter International Exposition, the Japanese Tea Garden endures as one of the most popular attractions in San Francisco, featuring classic elements such as an arched drum bridge, pagodas, stone lanterns, stepping stone paths, native Japanese plants, serene koi ponds, and a zen garden. Cherry blossom trees bloom throughout the garden in March and April.
Admission to the Japanese Tea Garden is free for San Francisco residents with valid ID. Free hours for everyone (even non-residents) are 9-10 am every Monday, Wednesday and Friday.

Please note that hours and costs change frequently.

Yerba Buena Center for the Arts
Opened to the public in 1993, YBCA was founded as the cultural anchor of San Francisco’s Yerba Buena Gardens neighborhood. Our work spans the realms of contemporary art, performance, film, civic engagement, and public life. Centering artists as essential to social and cultural movement, YBCA is reimagining the role an arts institution can play in the community it serves.
YBCA is located in the heart of San Francisco’s SOMA neighborhood, across the street from SFMOMA and the Moscone Convention Center. The main entrance to our galleries and forum event space is at 701 Mission Street. The main entrance to our theater is 700 Howard Street.

Rothmann.

From newspaper dispatches to television broadcasts, radio conversations and news delivered through smartphones, San Francisco’s media have chronicled a city defined by reinvention. Earthquakes, local politics, cultural movements, housing challenges and unforgettable personalities have provided generations of journalists with stories that resonate far beyond the Bay Area.

Japanese Tea Garden
The Japanese Tea Garden provides visitors from around the world with an opportunity to experience the natural beauty, tranquility, and harmony of a Japanese-style garden in the heart of San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park.
Originally created as a “Japanese Village” exhibit for the 1894 California Midwinter International Exposition, the Japanese Tea Garden endures as one of the most popular attractions in San Francisco, featuring classic elements such as an arched drum bridge, pagodas, stone lanterns, stepping stone paths, native Japanese plants, serene koi ponds, and a zen garden. Cherry blossom trees bloom throughout the garden in March and April.
Admission to the Japanese Tea Garden is free for San Francisco residents with valid ID. Free hours for everyone (even non-residents) are 9-10 am every Monday, Wednesday and Friday.

The Downtown express route make stops at the Presidio Transit Center on the Main Post, the Letterman District, Union Street/Van Ness Avenue, Embarcadero BART, and the Transbay Terminal.
The shuttle operates from 5:45 am to 9:30 pm on weekdays and 10 am to 7:30 pm on weekends. On weekdays, during the evening commute (leaving the Presidio only) from 4-7:40 pm, a valid MUNI Passport (not a MUNI Fast Pass) is required. No pass is required on weekends.
It’s free for Presidio Employees and Residents every day with an appropriate boarding pass. Connecting service to Caltrain is available.
The Downtown PresidiGo does not operate on federal holidays.
Around the Park (Every Day – 2 Routes)
Around the Park is free and available to visitors, residents, and employees all day. The shuttle runs two continuous 30-minute loops:

The Crissy Field Route serves the northern Presidio including the Main Post, Golden Gate Bridge, Fort Scott and Letterman District

Every third Saturday, you are invited to bicycle with the San Francisco Midnight Mystery Ride as they set out to a new mystery location in SF.
Where to meet? They’ll post ride start locations on their website and Facebook page, the day of the ride only; there’s no advance warning. The ride happens every third Saturday.
Participants are expected to:

Meet at a local bar before midnight on Saturday
Depart for a ride at midnight
Bring provisions for sharing at ride destination
Be awesome.

Ride start locations will be posted to their website the day of the ride. Only the ride leader knows where they’re going, so bring your sense of adventure. Rides are strictly NRLB (No Rider Left Behind) and generally around 5 miles – all levels of cyclist are welcome. They ride rain or shine.

Join RedBrick Ceramic Studio on Sunday, November 22 for a free artist talk and ceramic demonstration with artist Tasha Colby.

events.title: $1.50 Admission Day for Ripley’s Believe It or Not!’s Final Day in SF
events.venue: Ripley’s Believe It or Not Odditorium
events.description:
Google MapsRipley’s Believe It or Not! is closing its San Francisco Odditorium at Fisherman’s Wharf on Dec. 1, 2026, ending nearly 60 years of strange sights at 175 Jefferson St. The attraction first opened on Feb. 2, 1967, and it’s sending things off with a suitably weird farewell.
On its final day, admission will cost just $1.50 for adults and 75 cents for kids, matching the original 1967 ticket prices. Want to visit before then? Ripley’s is also offering $19.67 admission on Thursdays during its final weeks.
The museum is auctioning off select exhibits and artifacts through a silent auction that stays open until closing. Among the oddities up for grabs are a Golden Gate Bridge made on the head of a pin, toothpick replicas of the bridge, Joe DiMaggio’s crutches, a chicken-wire portrait of Janis Joplin, a matchstick cable car and even a fur-covered fish. There’s also a 1989 Emmy tied to coverage of the Loma Prieta earthquake and World Series.

The building is already being marketed for lease, so the future of this longtime Wharf attraction remains up in the air.
H/t SF Chronicle

GLBT History Museum
Located in SF’s Castro District, the GLBT Historical Society Museum is the first full-scale, stand-alone museum of its kind in the United States. The museum celebrates 100 years of the city’s vast queer past through dynamic exhibitions and programming.
Normally, admission is $10, but on the first Wednesday of every month, admission is free for everyone, thanks to a grant from the Bob Ross Foundation. Free tickets are not available for reservation online on free days; all visitors will be welcomed to the museum as long as there is capacity on a first-come, first-served basis.

events.title: San Francisco Bike Party (First Fridays)
events.description:
San Francisco Bike Party (First Fridays)
San Francisco Bike Party
San Francisco Bike Party (not to be confused with Critical Mass) is a monthly celebration of biking for riders of different ages, types, and skill levels to enjoy. Every month is a different theme and you’re encouraged to dress up.
San Francisco Bike Party is held on the first Friday at 8:00 pm every month (meet at 7:30p, roll at 8p). The starting location and route also changes every month. Check SF Bike Party’s Facebook page for updates.
The rides are fun and safe with stops to dance and socialize along the way. You’ll follow planned routes exploring all different parts of the city each month. They encourage people to bring positivity and contribute to good times while being respectful to others.

Who runs it? Created by a co-op, by and for bike enthusiasts, run by volunteers who plan the routes, test ride them, help participants ride in control, avoid traffic disruption, and not get lost. How SFBP rides: – Stay in the right lane – Stop at red lights – Leave no trace – Ride predictably and in control – Roll past conflict – Ride prepared – When in doubt, “bike party!!”
Updated 5/6/22 – Event info last checked via Facebook and Instagram

events.title: Drawing From Film—Night of the Hunter
events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerSFPLWe’ll be pausing Laughton’s Southern Gothic thriller, Night of the Hunter, to draw striking frames. We’ll be focusing on the art deco design, dramatic shadows and poses in the film.
Basic materials (pencils, paper, erasers) will be provided. You may bring your own materials, but please no fume-creating paint or paint pens. Watercolor, ink and gouache are fine.

This is a self-led event; there will be no instruction or feedback. However, there will be an opportunity at the end of the session to look at others’ drawings and show your own.
PG, 92 mins., 1955. Closed captions (CC) in English. Due to pauses for drawing, the full film will not be shown.
The event takes places in the Main Library at 100 Larkin Street, in the Latino/Hispanic Meeting Room.

Come enjoy the Afro-Cuban folkloric drums, dances, and songs of rumba. Rumba is the word used for a group of related, community-oriented, music and dance styles in Cuba.

Her poetry draws on her multiethnic background which includes Polish and Cherokee heritage, and her experiences as a lifelong resident of San Francisco. events.title: Hanukkah Klezmer Party with Veretski Pass
events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerCookie Segelstein
Celebrate Hanukkah with a rollicking klezmer concert at the Jazzschool, presented by legendary Bay Area klezmer trio Veretski Pass. Dust off your dancing shoes and come ready to move to the driving rhythms of traditional Jewish, Ukrainian, and Polish music, as well as original compositions and spirited improvisations in the klezmer tradition. Often raucous, always danceable!
Drawing on centuries-old Eastern European traditions, Veretski Pass offers a unique and exciting combination of virtuosic musicianship and raw energy that has excited audiences internationally for more than two decades. Instrumental in co-creating the “klezmer revival,” a movement which began in the 1970s with the goal of reviving Eastern European Jewish music, the band has performed and recorded hundreds of pieces of Jewish music, drawing on a vast array of sources, including contemporary and 19th-century ethnographic collections.

Performing on original instruments in an unbound, energetic “village style,” Veretski Pass has not only preserved, but reimagined, recomposed, and rearranged Jewish music from Ukraine, Poland, Carpathian-Ruthenia, Bessarabia, and Romania, enhancing and enriching modern klezmer music.

The free PresidiGo Shuttle system welcomes park visitors, residents, and employees with fully accessible shuttles and bike racks.

The Downtown express route make stops at the Presidio Transit Center on the Main Post, the Letterman District, Union Street/Van Ness Avenue, Embarcadero BART, and the Transbay Terminal.
The shuttle operates from 5:45 am to 9:30 pm on weekdays and 10 am to 7:30 pm on weekends. On weekdays, during the evening commute (leaving the Presidio only) from 4-7:40 pm, a valid MUNI Passport (not a MUNI Fast Pass) is required. No pass is required on weekends.
It’s free for Presidio Employees and Residents every day with an appropriate boarding pass. Connecting service to Caltrain is available.
The Downtown PresidiGo does not operate on federal holidays.
Around the Park (Every Day – 2 Routes)
Around the Park is free and available to visitors, residents, and employees all day. The shuttle runs two continuous 30-minute loops:

The Crissy Field Route serves the northern Presidio including the Main Post, Golden Gate Bridge, Fort Scott and Letterman District

events.description:
Submitted by the Event OrganizerAdam ShulmanJoin pianist Adam Shulman and his trio at the Jazzschool for a cozy holiday tribute to Bay Area jazz legend Vince Guaraldi and his iconic soundtrack to Charles Schulz’s 1965 TV special, A Charlie Brown Christmas. This event features two showtimes: an earlier family concert with a shortened runtime from 5:30-7pm, and a regular concert at 8pm.
Among the most beloved holiday albums of all time, A Charlie Brown Christmas has been certified Triple Platinum, was voted into the GRAMMY Hall of Fame in 2007, and was added to the Library of Congress’ National Recording Registry’s list of “culturally, historically, or aesthetically important” American recordings.

The album features a series of Christmas standards, including the Guaraldi originals “Christmas Time Is Here” and “Skating,” classic holiday songs like “O Tannenbaum” and “What Child Is This,” and the quintessential Peanuts Christmas tune, “Linus and Lucy.”
Pianist, composer, and arranger Adam Shulman has been a staple of the San Francisco jazz scene since he moved to the city in 2002. As a music student at UC Santa Cruz, Shulman studied jazz piano with the late, beloved piano master Smith Dobson, going on to work with internationally renowned artists such as Stefon Harris, Miguel Zenón, Luciana Souza, Paula West, Larry Coryell, Bobby Hutcherson, and the Glenn Miller Orchestra.

Every third Saturday, you are invited to bicycle with the San Francisco Midnight Mystery Ride as they set out to a new mystery location in SF.

First Tuesday of the month
On the first Tuesday of every month, admission to the permanent galleries is free (special exhibition fees still apply).

Free Things to See at the de Young
Even if you don’t attend on a free day, make sure to head up to the gorgeous glass-walled Hamon Observation Tower which offers stunning 360-degree panoramic views of downtown San Francisco, Golden Gate Park, the Bay, and the Marin headlands.
Also, stroll through the whimsical Barbro Osher Sculpture Garden to see modern works and James Turrel’s site-specific sculpture Skyspace.
Access to both the Observation Tower and the Sculpture Garden are free to the public. Please note, the Tower Observation Level closes one hour before the museum closes.

events.description:

Cartoon Art Museum
Founded in 1984, the Cartoon Art Museum has something for everyone—from comic strips, comic books and anime to political cartoons, graphic novels and underground comix. People of all ages can view original cartoon art at exhibitions and screenings, produce their own comics and animation at classes and workshops, research deeply into our collection and library, and mix and mingle with professional and aspiring cartoonists. This unique institution houses approximately 7,000 original pieces in our permanent collection and attracts more than 30,000 visitors annually.

Cartoon Art Museum, 781 Beach Street, San Francisco
FREE Admission
Pay What You Wish Days create affordable experiences for all to ignite imaginations and foster the next generation of visual storytellers by celebrating the history of cartoon art, its role in society, and its universal appeal with a visit to the Cartoon Art Museum.
